report.headline: Nearly one in five ALA koala remarks describes a sick, injured or dead animal, and 15 openly licensed iNaturalist sightings never reached ALA.

insights.title: One in five remarks describes a harmed koala
insights.essence: The keyword baseline labelled 19.3% of 3,631 ALA koala remarks as describing a sick, injured or dead koala, with disease named 431 times and vehicle strike 235 times.
insights.detail: Of the ALA remarks judged to be about a koala, 656 stated the animal was alive but unwell and 45 stated it was dead; disease was the most named event (431), ahead of vehicle strike (235), rescue or care (83), injury (24), with joey (35), dog attack (4) and fire (2). For carers and council staff this says the written record for NSW in 2016 is dominated by disease and road incidents rather than by dogs or fire. These are remarks describing harm, not a count of harmed animals.
insights.caveat: These figures come from the keyword baseline (regular expressions), which is approximate; no model classifier figures are in the pack. Condition was unknown for 2,812 of the 3,631 remarks, so most records say nothing either way.

insights.title: Fifteen open iNaturalist sightings missing from ALA
insights.essence: ALA holds 78.8% of iNaturalist's 80 NSW koala sightings; 17 are missing and 15 of those are openly licensed, so licensing explains only 11.8% of the gap.
insights.detail: Matching on the iNaturalist observation identifier, 63 sightings appear in both sources, 17 only in iNaturalist and 1 only in ALA. Only 2 of the missing records are all-rights-reserved; 13 are cc-by-nc and 1 cc-by-nc-nd, leaving an unexplained shortfall of 15. Anyone relying on ALA alone as the single NSW view will be missing a small but real slice of citizen-science records.
insights.caveat: The join only covers records carrying an iNaturalist identifier (80 on the iNaturalist side, 64 on the ALA side); it says nothing about flow from any other source, and the pack does not say why the 15 are absent.

insights.title: One dataset carries almost the whole picture
insights.essence: NSW BioNet Atlas supplies 4,728 of ALA's 5,226 records (90.5%) and 3,514 of its 3,572 substantive remarks, so the free-text signal is effectively one dataset's.
insights.detail: In the keyword pass, BioNet accounts for 3,549 of the 3,631 koala remarks, 654 of the 656 unwell, 428 of the 431 disease mentions and all 235 vehicle-strike mentions. The Australian Museum (304 records) and Tweed Koala Sightings (26 records) contribute no substantive occurrenceRemarks at all. Practitioners should treat the harm picture as a description of BioNet reporting practice, not of NSW reporting as a whole.
insights.caveat: Dataset shares describe where records come from, not where koalas are; a dataset with no remarks may still hold good location data.

insights.title: The two sources describe different kinds of sighting
insights.essence: Substantive remarks cover 68.4% of ALA records but only 27.5% of iNaturalist's, and the keyword harm share is 19.3% in ALA against 4.5% in iNaturalist.
insights.detail: ALA's text is dominated by a government atlas that records condition and incidents; iNaturalist's 22 labelled remarks include 10 alive and healthy, 1 dead, no vehicle strike and no unwell. This is consistent with ALA capturing rescue and incident reporting while iNaturalist captures opportunistic photographs of apparently healthy animals. Comparing harm rates between the two classifiers' outputs would confirm or refute this reading.
insights.caveat: iNaturalist's harm share rests on just 22 labelled remarks from 21 distinct texts, far too few to be stable; both figures come from the approximate keyword baseline.

insights.title: Obscuring is rare in ALA, common in iNaturalist
insights.essence: Only 1.1% of ALA records (58) sit beyond 10 km accuracy, against 27.5% of iNaturalist's (22 of 80) — deliberate privacy protection, not an error.
insights.detail: Median coordinate uncertainty is 30 m in NSW BioNet Atlas, 96 m in ALA's iNaturalist Australia feed and 122 m in iNaturalist itself, so most records are precise enough for site work. Of the 63 sightings matched across both sources, 14 are obscured on each side, meaning obscuring travels with the record rather than being added or removed in transfer. Plan fieldwork knowing a quarter of iNaturalist points are deliberately coarse.
insights.caveat: Medians hide the spread; a median of 30 m does not mean every BioNet record is that precise.

insights.title: Harvest is complete but georeferencing metadata is absent
insights.essence: Both sources reconciled fully (5,226 of 5,226 and 80 of 80), yet four georeferencing metadata flags fire on 100.0% of ALA records and coordinates are rounded on 69.4%.
insights.detail: Every ALA and iNaturalist record retrieved passed basic validation and both harvests are marked complete, so the counts are not truncated. But no ALA record carries a georeference date, georeferenced-by, georeference source or verification status, so there is no audit trail for how any point was derived. Treat positions as usable but unverifiable from this data alone.
insights.caveat: Missing metadata fields do not mean the coordinates themselves are wrong; rounding may be modest relative to the median uncertainties reported.

insights.title: Remarks peak in spring, road mentions in late winter
insights.essence: ALA koala remarks run from 215 in July to 434 in January, while vehicle-strike mentions peak at 34 in August and 33 in October and fall to 7 in March.
insights.detail: Monthly disease mentions are highest in December (59) and October (46) and lowest in February (25). Vehicle-strike mentions sit at 24 in June, 32 in July, 34 in August and 33 in October, well above the 7 to 16 seen from January to May. This points to when to time road-safety messaging and carer rostering, though it reflects when people reported and wrote remarks as much as when incidents happened.
insights.caveat: Monthly counts track reporting and remark-writing effort, not koala numbers or incident rates; a single year and the approximate keyword baseline cannot establish a seasonal pattern.
